meta.title: Who really said "Often we are so busy with sawing that we forget to sharpen the saw"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wikiquote files this wording under Disputed, uncited. Covey's real printed line: "We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Often we are so busy with sawing that we forget to sharpen the saw'?
meta.ogDescription: The thought is genuinely Stephen Covey's. The words are not. His documented sentence reads differently, and this version has no source at all.

answer.label: Not Covey’s words — a paraphrase of his real line
answer.authorDates: 1932–2012 · American educator, businessman & author of The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
answer.sourceLine: The idea belongs to Covey — it is the whole of his seventh habit, which FranklinCovey still publishes as “Sharpen the Saw®” ↗. The sentence does not. Covey’s own aphorism, in print since 1970, runs “We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw.” This reworded version carries no citation anywhere: Wikiquote files it under Disputed ↗, and Open Library’s full-text search of scanned books returns no match at all ↗.
answer.confidenceText: The idea is Covey’s; this sentence is not

source.heading: What Covey actually wrote — and what this is

docMeta.dd: “Often we are so busy with sawing that we forget to sharpen the saw” — no citation has ever been attached to it
Listed under Disputed on Wikiquote; no match in Open Library’s full-text book corpus
“We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw.”
Spiritual Roots of Human Relations (Deseret Book, 1970)

source.excerpt: “…come upon someone in the woods working feverishly to saw down a tree. ‘What are you doing?’ you…” [the exchange runs on, and closes:] “‘I don’t have time to sharpen the saw,’ the man says emphatically. ‘I’m too busy sawing.’” [And Covey’s own aphorism for the habit, carried in his books since 1970:] “We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw.”
trail: Before Covey — the underlying proverb is older than any of his books and belongs to nobody in particular. Quote Investigator traces the axe form to a 1944 speech by Reverend W. H. Alexander, who credited an anonymous lumberjack ↗, and states flatly that “there is no substantive evidence that Abraham Lincoln who died in 1865 made a remark of this type.” QI’s article covers the axe only — it does not mention a saw version or Covey.

1970 — Covey states the idea in his own words in his first book, Spiritual Roots of Human Relations: “We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw.” Open Library’s full-text search on the core phrase finds it there and, in small variants, across several later Covey titles ↗. (No source traces a line from the axe proverb to Covey’s saw wording — the adjacency here is chronological, not a documented derivation.)

1989 — The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People makes it Habit 7 and adds the parable everyone now remembers, of the man “working feverishly to saw down a tree” who answers “I’m too busy sawing.” The passage is searchable in Covey’s own Renewal and The Wisdom and Teachings of Stephen R. Covey ↗.

Today — the reworded sentence circulates as a Covey quotation with no book, page or date behind it. Wikiquote keeps it in Disputed, uncited ↗, and aggregators copy it out from there — QuotePark reprints it and says outright that it was “adopted from Wikiquote” ↗.
source.cutTag: Fragments as returned by Open Library’s full-text search
source.excerptNote: Read the two side by side and the difference is the whole case. Covey’s sentence is an instruction with a hinge in it — never become too busy sawing to take time — and the parable it caps is a dialogue, with the punchline in the woodcutter’s mouth rather than the author’s. The circulating version flattens both into a soft observation about what “we” forget, and drops the word Covey leaned on: time. It also arrives with a tell. Wikiquote records it with a doubled full stop — “sharpen the saw..” — the kind of artefact that comes from a list being copied between databases, not from a book being transcribed.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this exact sentence, because nobody has identified who wrote it or where it first appeared — it is an anonymous rewording with no located source, and a quotation that cannot be traced cannot be declared public domain. The wording it derives from is a different matter: Covey’s “We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw” is published text from Spiritual Roots of Human Relations (Deseret Book, 1970) and The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (Simon & Schuster, 1989), both firmly inside US copyright, which is why this page quotes only the short passages under examination.

author.name: Stephen Covey
author.heading: Who was Stephen Covey?
author.bio: Stephen Richards Covey (24 October 1932 – 16 July 2012) was an American educator, businessman and motivational speaker whose 1989 book The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People became one of the most widely read business books ever published. Long before it, he was writing for a Latter-day Saint readership — Spiritual Roots of Human Relations appeared from Deseret Book in 1970, and it already contains the sawing aphorism in the form he would use for the rest of his career. Habit 7, “Sharpen the Saw,” is what this quotation is reaching for: the argument that time spent renewing yourself is not time stolen from the work.

cite.sourceCitation: No source exists for the popular wording: Wikiquote, “Stephen Covey,” lists it under Disputed without citation, and Open Library’s full-text search returns no match. The closest documented original is Stephen R. Covey, Spiritual Roots of Human Relations (Salt Lake City: Deseret Book, 1970): “We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw.” The parable form appears in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (New York: Simon & Schuster, 1989), Habit 7.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong name on the right words. The name is right — the idea is Covey’s, down to the metaphor — and the words are wrong. That combination is unusually hard to catch, because everything about the sentence checks out except the sentence.

items.why: Nobody has produced a book, page, speech or date for this exact sentence. Wikiquote keeps it in the Disputed block ↗, under a header note explaining that those entries were added to an article for First Things First and moved across, and that “many originally among them have already been found to have been paraphrases, rather than exact quotations.” The sibling entries in that same block — “No gardener, no garden!”, “Until you live, learn how to live.”, “Wisdom is synergy of mind and heart.” — share its slightly off-kilter English.

Full-text search across Open Library’s scanned corpus finds nothing at all for the phrase “so busy with sawing” ↗ — not in Covey, not in anyone. The same kind of search run on the core of Covey’s real sentence — “too busy sawing to take time to sharpen” — returns about twenty-five books ↗, several of them his own. A line he supposedly wrote should not be absent from every book ever scanned.

Sites recycle the Wikiquote list and quietly drop the “disputed” qualifier, or attach a book to it that nobody checked. QuotePark reprints the line, states it was “adopted from Wikiquote,” and pins it to First Things First (1994) ↗ — a title inherited from the Wikiquote section’s own editorial history, not from anyone finding the sentence inside the book.

The sharpen-your-blade idea is often served up as Lincoln’s — the six-hours-to-chop-a-tree line — and dropped alongside Covey’s habit as though the two were a matched pair. Quote Investigator finds the earliest instance in 1944, credited to an anonymous lumberjack, and states there is “no substantive evidence” Lincoln said anything of the type ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Stephen Covey built an entire habit on this thought, and wrote it down plainly: “We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw” ↗. The version on the poster is somebody else’s rewrite of that line, and no one has ever said whose.

context.heading: Why this one slips through
lead: Most misattributions fail an obvious test — the person was already dead, or the sentiment is nothing like anything they ever wrote. This one passes every obvious test. Covey really did use this metaphor, really did make it the climax of The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, and really did phrase it as a warning about being too busy. The sentence sounds like him because it is a copy of something he said. It simply is not the thing he said.

What gets lost in the copying is the part that did the work. Covey’s line is about time — refusing to let the work crowd out the maintenance that makes the work possible — and his parable puts the excuse into a character’s mouth so you can hear how ridiculous it sounds out loud. The rewrite turns a refusal into an oversight. We do not forget to sharpen the saw. Covey’s woodcutter knows exactly where the file is and says he is too busy.
context.detailsSummary: The paper trail behind Covey’s version
detailsBody: The aphorism is older in Covey’s work than most readers assume. It is not a 7 Habits invention: Open Library’s full-text search finds it in Spiritual Roots of Human Relations ↗, the book he published with Deseret Book in 1970, and it recurs across his later titles including The Divine Center, Principle-Centered Leadership and The Wisdom and Teachings of Stephen R. Covey, with small variations — “never become,” “never get” — that are Covey’s own.

The parable is the durable part. Its opening — coming “upon someone in the woods working feverishly to saw down a tree” — is searchable in Covey’s own Renewal ↗ and has been reprinted in dozens of unrelated books on ministry, teaching, healthcare management and marketing, which is a fair measure of how far Habit 7 travelled.

The idea itself belongs to no one. Quote Investigator’s chronology of the axe version ↗ starts in 1944 with Reverend W. H. Alexander invoking an anonymous lumberjack who, given five minutes to fell a tree, would spend three of them sharpening. The Lincoln credit came later and has nothing behind it. Covey’s contribution was not the proverb but the frame he built around it.
context.pull: “We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw.” — Stephen Covey’s actual sentence, in print since 1970

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Stephen Covey page carries "Often we are so busy with sawing that we forget to sharpen the saw.." verbatim in its Disputed section, with no citation, under a header note saying the entries were added to an article for First Things First and transferred, and that many "have already been found to have been paraphrases, rather than exact quotations." No sawing line appears in the page's sourced sections.
Open Library's full-text search of scanned books returns zero matches for the phrase "so busy with sawing" ("No Search Inside text matched your search").

Open Library's full-text search returns "About 25 results found" for the core phrase "too busy sawing to take time to sharpen", including three scans of Stephen R. Covey's Spiritual Roots of Human Relations ("We must never become too busy sawing to take time to sharpen the saw."), The Divine Center, four editions of Principle-Centered Leadership, How to Succeed with People, two editions of The Wisdom and Teachings of Stephen R. Covey, and Sean Covey's The 7 Habits of Happy Kids and 6 Most Important Decisions You'll Ever Make, alongside unrelated books quoting the line.

Searched verbatim, Covey's sentence returns "About 6 results found": three scans of Spiritual Roots of Human Relations, two editions of The Wisdom and Teachings of Stephen R. Covey, and one non-Covey title (Poelman, How to Make a Difference). The Divine Center, Principle-Centered Leadership and the Sean Covey titles carry variant wording ("never get") and appear only under the looser query.

Open Library's full-text search for "I don't have time to sharpen the saw" returns 52 books, including Stephen R. Covey's Renewal: Nourishing Body, Mind, Heart, and Soul with the snippet "'I don't have time to sharpen the saw,' the man says emphatically...".

Open Library's full-text search for "working feverishly to saw down a tree" returns Stephen R. Covey's Renewal and The Wisdom and Teachings of Stephen R. Covey among the results, with the snippet "come upon someone in the woods working feverishly to saw down a tree. 'What are you doing?' you".

Quote Investigator traces the axe-sharpening saying to a 1944 speech by Reverend W. H. Alexander crediting an anonymous lumberjack ("if his life depended upon his ability to cut down a tree in five minutes he would spend three minutes sharpening his axe"), and states "There is no substantive evidence that Abraham Lincoln who died in 1865 made a remark of this type." The article does not mention a saw version or Stephen Covey.

FranklinCovey's own site names the seventh habit "Sharpen the Saw®" and describes it as preserving and enhancing ourselves across body, heart, mind and spirit; the page carries a different Covey quotation and no woodcutter parable.

Wikipedia gives Stephen Covey's dates as born 24 October 1932 and died 16 July 2012, describes him as an American educator, author, businessman and motivational speaker, dates The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People to 1989, and lists Spiritual Roots of Human Relations (1970, Deseret Book Company) among his early books.

QuotePark reprints "Often we are so busy with sawing that we forget to sharpen the saw.." credited to Stephen R. Covey, marks it "Disputed", states it was "Adopted from Wikiquote", and cites First Things First (1994) as the work.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of Stephen R. Covey's Spiritual Roots of Human Relations, published by Deseret Book Co., Salt Lake City, 1970.
